summary: Describes a deployed extension to RADIUS that lets a server change a user session after it has begun, including disconnecting a user and changing the authorizations that apply. It documents what network access server products already did. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 5176.

eli5.summary: Normally a login server only answers when asked. This memo lets it tell a network box, while someone is online, to cut them off or change what they can do.

questions: how to disconnect a radius user mid-session
subtitle: Server-initiated commands to disconnect users and update their permissions mid-session.

tldr.problem: RADIUS servers can only respond to requests from the network access server (NAS), not initiate commands. Administrators need to disconnect users or change their permissions while they are online.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC extends RADIUS with two new message types: Disconnect-Request (to terminate a session) and Change-of-Authorization messages (to modify session attributes like data filters), both sent from the server to the NAS on UDP port 3799.
tldr.outcome: The extension documents what vendors had already implemented in practice, enabling dynamic session management. It was later replaced by RFC 5176 with improved security and semantic clarity.

today: RFC 5176 is the current standard for dynamic authorization extensions to RADIUS. RFC 3576 is documented as its informational predecessor and is still deployed in many networks.

sections.title: The Problem with Passive RADIUS
sections.content:
The RADIUS protocol (Remote Authentication Dial In User Service) allows a network access server to ask a RADIUS server if a user should be allowed to log in. However, RADIUS only supports request-reply exchanges where the NAS asks and the server answers. It has no way for the server to send unsolicited messages, such as telling the NAS to disconnect a user or to change what that user is allowed to do.

In practice, administrators need to take action mid-session: perhaps to enforce a policy change, disconnect a user who violated rules, or update bandwidth limits. This extension adds that capability, documenting what several vendors had already deployed.
sections.eli5: Normally you can only ask the login server questions and wait for answers. This adds a way for the server to send orders without being asked, like 'disconnect that user now' or 'let them do something new'.

sections.title: Two New Message Types
sections.content:
The extension defines two kinds of server-initiated messages, both sent to UDP port 3799 instead of the normal RADIUS port:

Disconnect-Request tells the NAS to terminate a user session and discard all related data. The NAS responds with either Disconnect-ACK (if successful) or Disconnect-NAK (if it cannot disconnect the session). The request includes identification attributes such as the user name and the NAS address so the NAS can find the right session.

Change-of-Authorization (CoA) messages modify authorizations for an active session, such as applying a data filter or changing the user's access level. The NAS responds with CoA-ACK (if all changes apply) or CoA-NAK (if any change cannot be made). If a CoA request fails, no changes are applied—changes must be atomic.
sections.eli5: The server can send two kinds of orders: 'drop this person's connection' or 'change what this person can do'. The network box says 'done' or 'can't do it'.

sections.title: Packet Structure and Codes
sections.content:
Disconnect and CoA messages use the same packet structure as standard RADIUS: a Code field (one byte), an Identifier (one byte), a Length field, a 16-byte Authenticator (MD5 checksum), and attributes in Type-Length-Value format. Six new packet codes are defined: Disconnect-Request (40), Disconnect-ACK (41), Disconnect-NAK (42), CoA-Request (43), CoA-ACK (44), and CoA-NAK (45).

The Authenticator is computed the same way as in RADIUS Accounting, not as in Access-Request. The Identifier field helps match requests with responses, and the server (not the NAS) is responsible for retransmitting if no reply arrives. If the server retransmits with identical attributes, it must use the same Identifier; if attributes change, a new Identifier and Authenticator are required.
sections.eli5: The messages look like regular RADIUS packets with headers and labels. The authenticator is a checksum that proves the message came from the right server, and a number in the identifier helps match questions with answers.

sections.title: Session Identification and Error Reporting
sections.content:
Disconnect and CoA messages must identify the NAS and the session they apply to. NAS identification attributes include the NAS IP address, NAS IPv6 address, or NAS identifier string. Session identification attributes include the user name, NAS port, framed IP address, and the session ID—a unique number the NAS assigned to each session.

All attributes in Disconnect and CoA messages are treated as mandatory; if the NAS does not support any attribute or attribute value, it must send a NAK. The RFC also defines an Error-Cause attribute with numeric codes to explain why a request failed, such as 'Session Context Not Found', 'Unsupported Attribute', or 'Administratively Prohibited'.
sections.eli5: The messages include labels identifying who the user is and where they are connected—their name, the network box's address, and a session number. If something goes wrong, an error code explains why.

sections.title: Protecting Against Misuse
sections.content:
The RFC acknowledges several security vulnerabilities in deployed implementations. One risk is that a NAS shared by multiple Internet service providers could be tricked into disconnecting another provider's users. The RFC recommends a 'reverse path forwarding' check: the NAS should verify that a Disconnect or CoA message came from an authorized RADIUS server for that user's realm.

Another vulnerability is that a rogue NAS could forge the source IP address in a request to trick the server into sending attacks to an innocent NAS. The RFC recommends that proxies and servers verify that NAS identification attributes match the source address of packets. To address weak authentication in older RADIUS implementations, IPsec is recommended, and for replay attacks, the Event-Timestamp attribute should be included with a default time window of 300 seconds.
sections.eli5: A bad actor could trick the system in a few ways: pretending to be the right server, lying about which network box is asking, or replaying old messages. Use IPsec to encrypt the messages, check that things match up, and add timestamps so old orders are ignored.

sections.title: Status and Successor
sections.content:
RFC 5176 obsoletes this document. This RFC is marked Informational rather than Standards Track because of semantic ambiguities in how CoA attributes identify sessions versus authorize changes—a problem that Diameter, its successor protocol, addresses more cleanly. The specification also documents known security weaknesses, such as the lack of authorization checks in early implementations, that cannot be fixed without breaking compatibility.

Despite these limitations, Disconnect and CoA messages are widely deployed for managing user sessions and enforcing policy changes in real-world networks, and RFC 5176 provides the updated specification.
sections.eli5: A newer RFC, 5176, fixes some of the confusing parts and better security. Both versions are used in real networks today.
